These notes review the probability and statistical concepts used throughout
time-series econometrics. The emphasis is on random variables, dependence,
sampling, likelihood-based estimation, and the distinction between frequentist
and Bayesian inference.

## Recap: From Probability to Statistical Inference — Three Coin Tosses

### Recap :From Probability to Statistical Inference 

| Concept | In this example |
|:---|:---|
| **Experiment** | Toss three coins |
| **Sample space** | $\{HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT\}$ |
| **Event** | Exactly two Heads: $\{HHT, HTH, THH\}$ |
| **Random variable** | $X =$ number of Heads |
| **Probability distribution** | $X \sim \text{Binomial}(3, 0.5)$ |
| **Population** | Possible observations generated by repeated experiments |
| **Parameter** | $p = 0.5,\quad \mu = E(X) = 1.5$ |
| **Sample** | $\{2, 1, 3, 2, 0\}$ |
| **Sample statistic** | $\bar X = 1.6,\quad \hat p = 8/15$ |

## Estimators and their properties

An **estimator** $\hat\theta$ is a rule (a function of the sample data) used to
estimate an unknown population parameter $\theta$. Because it depends on a random
sample, $\hat\theta$ is itself a random variable and has a **sampling
distribution**. Its quality is judged by the location and spread of that
distribution.

* **Bias:**
  $$
  \operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E(\hat\theta) - \theta.
  $$
  The estimator is **unbiased** if $E(\hat\theta) = \theta$, i.e. it does not
  systematically over- or under-estimate the parameter across repeated samples.

* **Efficiency:** among unbiased estimators, the one with the smaller variance is
  more precise, and is preferred.

* **Consistency:** as the sample size grows, the estimator concentrates on the
  truth, $\hat\theta \xrightarrow{p} \theta$.

* **Asymptotic unbiasedness:** any bias vanishes as $n \to \infty$,
  $\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta) \to 0$.

* **Asymptotic normality:** for many estimators,
  $$
  \sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, V),
  $$
  which justifies approximate confidence intervals and hypothesis tests in large
  samples.

* **Standard error:** the (estimated) standard deviation of $\hat\theta$'s
  sampling distribution. It measures sampling uncertainty and is the basis of
  confidence intervals and tests.

Popular methods for constructing estimators include **least squares**,
**method of moments**, and **maximum likelihood**.

| Method | Main idea |
|:---|:---|
| **Least squares (LS)** | Choose parameters that make fitted values close to observed values in squared-error terms |
| **Method of moments (MoM)** | Choose parameters so model-implied moments match sample moments |
| **Maximum likelihood (ML)** | Choose parameters under which the observed data are most compatible with the probability model |

## Frequentist inference: uncertainty through repeated sampling

In the frequentist framework, the parameter $\theta$ is treated as **fixed but
unknown**. The sample is random, so the estimator is random before the data are
observed.

The basic logic is

$$
\text{probability model}
\longrightarrow
\text{estimator } \hat\theta
\longrightarrow
\text{sampling distribution of } \hat\theta.
$$

From the sampling distribution we obtain the main tools of frequentist inference.

### Standard error

The **standard error** measures the typical sampling variation of an estimator.
A small standard error means the estimator is relatively precise.

### Confidence interval

A 95% confidence-interval procedure is constructed so that, under repeated
sampling, approximately 95% of intervals produced by that procedure contain the
true parameter.

Once an interval has been calculated from the observed sample, the standard
frequentist interpretation does **not** assign a 95% probability to the fixed
parameter being inside that particular interval.

### Hypothesis test and p-value

A hypothesis test asks whether the observed statistic would be unusual if a null
hypothesis were true. The **p-value** is the probability, under the null model,
of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one.

It is **not** the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
